takeaways: CO comes from too little oxygen, HC from fuel the flame never reaches (crevices first), and NO from a hot flame with spare oxygen; NO peaks near φ = 0.9.
Soot forms in the hot rich core of a diesel spray and mostly burns out; PM is what survives plus SOF, sulphate and ash, and it trades against NOx.

In-cylinder methods (retard, EGR, injection strategy) stop pollutants forming; after-treatment converts them, and a lean diesel needs DOC, DPF and SCR because a three-way catalyst works only at λ = 1.
Each gas is measured by its own physics: infrared absorption, ozone chemiluminescence, flame ionisation and light extinction; a ppm reading becomes g/km or g/kWh only through mass.
A limit means nothing without its cycle: India’s cars are tested on the 11.0 km MIDC and held to BS-VI limits equal to Euro 6.
Gas fuels cut CO₂ per MJ (methane 22 % below petrol) but carry four to seven times less energy per litre of tank.
A dual-fuel engine lights a lean gas charge with a diesel pilot; it knocks at high load and slips methane at light load.
A stratified charge engine fires a rich zone in a lean charge to drop the throttle; an LHR engine insulates the chamber, but most of the saved heat goes to the exhaust.
HCCI and RCCI keep every parcel lean and below about 2000 K to avoid both soot and NOx; RCCI uses two fuels of different reactivity as its control lever.
bank_note: Long questions on the advanced engines usually ask for a neat sketch and an explanation: the stratified charge chamber, the insulated LHR chamber and the φ–T map with HCCI and RCCI. Most syllabi that teach emissions ask for formation, the analysers and the after-treatment line; numerical questions come from EGR rate, specific emissions and dual-fuel substitution.

bank.q: Explain how carbon monoxide, unburnt hydrocarbons and oxides of nitrogen form in a spark-ignition engine, and show how the equivalence ratio affects each.
outline: CO: too little oxygen on the rich side; dissociation and frozen CO oxidation in expansion
HC: crevices (largest), oil film, quench layer, liquid fuel and misfire, valve overlap; partial burn-up in expansion and exhaust
NOx: thermal NO by the Zeldovich mechanism; needs high temperature, oxygen atoms and time
Effect of φ: CO and HC high rich, NO peaks near φ = 0.9, HC rises again at lean misfire
Sketch of the three curves against air–fuel ratio
answer: Define the mixture: φ = actual fuel–air ratio ÷ stoichiometric fuel–air ratio. For petrol the stoichiometric air–fuel ratio is about 14.7, so φ = 1.1 is an air–fuel ratio of 13.4 and φ = 0.9 one of 16.3.

CO formation. Carbon in the fuel first forms CO, which burns on to CO2 mainly by CO + OH → CO2 + H. On the rich side (φ > 1) there is not enough oxygen to finish this step, so CO rises steeply with richness, to a few per cent at φ = 1.2. Near stoichiometric, hot burned gas holds some CO from the dissociation CO2 ⇌ CO + ½O2; as the gas cools in expansion the CO-burning reactions slow and freeze, leaving a few tenths of a per cent. In lean mixtures CO is low.

HC formation. HC is fuel that escapes the flame. (i) Crevices: the top-land gap, ring grooves and plug thread fill with mixture during compression; the flame cannot enter a gap this narrow, and the gas returns during expansion. This is the largest source. (ii) Oil film: fuel vapour dissolves in the liner oil at high pressure and comes out after the flame. (iii) Wall quenching: the flame dies about 0.1 mm from cold walls. (iv) Liquid fuel on cold walls and misfire, mainly at cold start. (v) Valve overlap: some fresh charge short-circuits to the exhaust. Part of this HC burns in the hot gas during expansion and in the exhaust port, which is why spark retard lowers HC.

NOx formation. Thermal NO forms in the burned gas behind the flame by the Zeldovich mechanism: O + N2 → NO + N, N + O2 → NO + O, extended by N + OH → NO + H. The first step breaks the N≡N bond, so the rate rises very steeply above about 1800 K. NO therefore needs high peak temperature, oxygen atoms and residence time. Prompt NO in the flame front and fuel nitrogen add small amounts. In a petrol engine NO is almost all of the NOx.

answer.text: Effect of the equivalence ratio (the sketch shows the trends):

answer: Sketch: three curves against air–fuel ratio 10 to 20; CO falls steeply from the rich side and flattens past 15; HC falls and rises again beyond about 18; NO is a hump peaking near 16.3, with a narrow band at 14.7 marking the three-way catalyst window.
Other variables: spark advance, compression ratio and load raise peak temperature and NO; EGR and retard lower NO; a cold engine raises HC and CO.

Conclusion: the three gases come from three different failures (oxygen shortage, fuel hidden from the flame, an over-hot flame), so no single setting of φ minimises all three. This is why petrol engines are held at λ = 1 and finished with a three-way catalyst.

bank.q: Describe the formation of soot in a diesel spray, and explain the difference between smoke, particulate matter and the soluble organic fraction. How is PM measured?
outline: Rich core φ 2 to 4, 1600–2600 K
Pyrolysis, nucleation, surface growth, coagulation, agglomeration, oxidation
PM = soot + SOF + sulphate + ash; smoke is the visible soot
Smoke colours and causes
Gravimetric PM with dilution at 47 °C; opacimeter and filter smoke number
answer: Where soot forms: in a diesel spray the liquid core evaporates into a region where the local equivalence ratio is 2 to 4 and the temperature 1600 to 2600 K. There is too little oxygen to burn the fuel, so it breaks down instead.

Six steps. (1) Pyrolysis: fuel molecules crack into small pieces such as acetylene and build polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAH). (2) Nucleation: PAH stick into the first particles of 1 to 2 nm. (3) Surface growth: acetylene adds to the surface; mass rises fast. (4) Coagulation: small spheres merge into primary particles of 10 to 30 nm. (5) Agglomeration: the spheres stick into chains a few hundred nm long. (6) Oxidation: when the jet mixes with air, OH and O2 burn the soot. Most of the soot formed is burnt; exhaust soot is what survives step 6.

Particulate matter is defined by measurement: all material caught on a filter from diluted exhaust at 47 °C. It contains soot (dry carbon), the soluble organic fraction (unburnt fuel and lubricating oil that condense on the soot, often half the mass at light load), sulphate with bound water (from fuel sulphur) and ash (from oil additives).

Smoke is the visible part. Black smoke is soot from too much fuel for the air; blue smoke is burning lubricating oil; white smoke is unburnt fuel droplets or water vapour, typical of a cold start. A clear exhaust can still carry SOF and sulphate, so smoke and PM are not the same.

Gravimetric PM measurement. A sample of exhaust is diluted with filtered air (full-flow CVS or partial flow), cooled to 47 °C so the SOF condenses as it would in the air, and drawn through a conditioned filter. The filter is weighed on a microbalance before and after. Worked figure: 0.90 mg on the filter from 0.30 m³ of gas diluted 8 times gives 3.0 × 8 = 24 mg/m³ raw; with 0.05 m³/s of exhaust that is 1.2 mg/s, and at 40 kW, 4.32 g/h ÷ 40 = 0.108 g/kWh.

Smoke measurement. An opacimeter passes light across the exhaust and reports opacity N or the absorption coefficient k = −ln(1 − N) ÷ L; 45 % opacity on a 0.430 m path is k = 1.39 m⁻¹. A filter-paper meter reads the blackness of paper after a fixed volume as a Bosch or filter smoke number (0 to 10). Both see mainly soot.
Factors: higher injection pressure, swirl and low-sulphur fuel lower PM; higher load, retard and EGR raise it. Retard and EGR are the NOx controls, which gives the NOx–PM trade-off.
Conclusion: soot is born in the rich core and mostly burnt later; PM adds the liquid and ash parts and must be weighed, while smoke meters see only the black part.

bank.q: Classify emission control methods into in-cylinder treatments and after-treatment, and describe four devices or methods of each class.
outline: In-cylinder: retard, EGR, injection strategy, λ control, chamber design, crankcase and evaporative control
After-treatment: TWC, DOC, DPF, SCR, LNT
Reaction or mechanism and operating window of each
Matching to petrol and diesel engines
The two classes are used together
answer: Classification: in-cylinder methods reduce what the engine forms; after-treatment converts or traps it between the exhaust valve and the tailpipe. Modern engines need both.
In-cylinder 1, spark or injection retard: the burn moves later, the peak temperature falls and NO falls; costs fuel, and in a diesel raises PM.

In-cylinder 2, exhaust gas recirculation: exhaust in the intake replaces oxygen and adds CO2 and H2O, which absorb heat, so the flame is cooler. Rate = (CO2 intake − CO2 ambient) ÷ (CO2 exhaust − CO2 ambient); with 0.04, 1.80 and 12.0 % it is 14.7 %. Cooled EGR packs more mass; too much raises PM and HC.
In-cylinder 3, injection strategy (CI): high common-rail pressure for fine sprays; pilot injection to shorten the delay and soften the premixed burst; post injection to burn soot or heat the filter.

In-cylinder 4, closed-loop λ control and chamber design (SI): an oxygen sensor holds λ = 1 for the catalyst; a compact chamber with small crevices lowers HC. Crankcase ventilation returns blow-by gas to the intake, and a charcoal canister holds tank vapour.

After-treatment 1, three-way catalyst: Pt, Pd, Rh on a honeycomb; CO + ½O2 → CO2, HC + O2 → CO2 + H2O, 2NO + 2CO → N2 + 2CO2. Works only within about ±0.5 % of λ = 1 and above light-off, about 250 to 300 °C.
After-treatment 2, diesel oxidation catalyst: burns CO, HC and part of the SOF in lean exhaust and turns NO into NO2 for the next devices.

After-treatment 3, diesel particulate filter: a wall-flow honeycomb with alternate channels plugged; gas passes through porous walls and soot stays. Passive regeneration by NO2 at 250 to 400 °C, active at about 600 °C with a post injection; ash remains.

After-treatment 4, selective catalytic reduction: AdBlue (32.5 % urea) gives NH3; 4NH3 + 4NO + O2 → 4N2 + 6H2O; works from about 200 °C; a slip catalyst removes leftover ammonia. The lean NOx trap is the alternative: it stores nitrate while lean and is purged rich.

head: Engine
Line
rows: DOC → DPF → urea → SCR → slip catalyst

answer: Conclusion: in-cylinder methods usually trade one pollutant against another (retard and EGR: NOx down, PM up); after-treatment removes the remainder, and low-sulphur fuel keeps it working.

bank.q: With neat sketches, explain the working of the NDIR analyser, the chemiluminescence NOx analyser, the flame ionisation detector and a smoke meter.
outline: NDIR: source, chopper, sample and reference cells, gas-filled detector; CO 4.7 µm, CO₂ 4.3 µm; Beer–Lambert
CLD: NO + O₃ → NO₂* + O₂; photomultiplier; converter for NO₂; η correction
FID: hydrogen flame, ion current ∝ carbon atoms, ppmC; heated
Smoke meters: opacimeter (k) and filter paper (Bosch number)
What each cannot measure
answer: Sample handling first: probe, heated line at about 190 °C, soot filter; the FID takes hot wet gas; NDIR and CLD take dried gas; the smoke meter takes raw exhaust.

NDIR (CO, CO2). Sketch: infrared source → rotating chopper → sample cell and reference cell side by side → detector chamber filled with the gas to be measured → amplifier and meter. The chopper alternates the beam; the gas-filled detector absorbs only the wavelengths of its own gas (CO near 4.7 µm, CO2 near 4.3 µm), so the difference between the two beams measures that gas without a prism. Absorption follows Beer–Lambert, I = I0e−acL; for example, a span gas of 2.0 % CO passing 70 % of the light and a sample passing 80 % give c = 2.0 × ln 0.80 ÷ ln 0.70 = 1.25 % CO. Water absorbs in the infrared, so the sample is dried.

Chemiluminescence analyser (NO, NOx). Sketch: sample → switching valve (bypass or NO2→NO converter) → reaction chamber fed with ozone from an ozone generator → optical filter → photomultiplier → meter. NO + O3 → NO2* + O2; the excited molecule emits light in proportion to NO. Bypass gives NO; through the converter gives NOx. With 380 and 420 ppm and converter efficiency 0.92, NO2 = 40 ÷ 0.92 = 43.5 ppm and NOx = 423.5 ppm. Water and CO2 quench the light, so the sample is dried.

Flame ionisation detector (HC). Sketch: sample and hydrogen fuel mixed → burner jet with air → collector electrode around the flame with a polarising voltage → electrometer. Organic carbon forms ions in the flame; the current is proportional to the number of carbon atoms, so the reading is ppmC (one ppm propane ≈ 3 ppmC). The FID is heated to about 190 °C so heavy HC do not condense; it does not see CO, CO2 or water and under-reads oxygenates.

Smoke meters. Opacimeter (Hartridge type): a lamp and a photocell at the ends of a tube through which exhaust flows; opacity N = share of light blocked; k = −ln(1 − N) ÷ L. Filter-paper (Bosch) meter: a pump draws a fixed volume through white paper; a reflectometer reads the blackening on a 0 to 10 scale. Both respond mainly to soot, not PM mass.

head: Analyser
Gas
Principle
Blind to
rows: NO at low ppm, most HC, O<sub>2</sub>

answer: Oxygen is measured by a paramagnetic analyser. Every analyser is set with a zero gas (nitrogen) and a span gas of known concentration.
Conclusion: each gas is measured by a physical effect of its own, and each method has a blind spot that the bench layout must cover.

bank.q: What is a stratified charge engine? With a neat sketch, explain the working of a divided-chamber (pre-chamber) stratified charge engine and of a direct-injection stratified engine, and list their merits and demerits.
outline: Rich at the plug, lean overall; quality control of load, throttle open
Ignition limits of a homogeneous mixture and pumping loss
Divided chamber (CVCC): third valve, rich pre-chamber, flame jets
Open chamber DI: TCCS, PROCO; wall-, air-, spray-guided GDI
Merits: efficiency, low CO, lean knock margin; demerits: HC, soot, NOx without TWC, complexity
answer: Definition: a stratified charge has a mixture strength that varies through the chamber, rich (φ about 1 to 1.3) at the spark plug and lean elsewhere, so the charge is lean overall (air–fuel ratio 20 to 40 or more).

Why: a homogeneous petrol mixture can be ignited only between about φ = 0.7 and 1.3. A normal engine therefore keeps φ near 1 and reduces the quantity with a throttle. The throttle causes pumping loss. Worked figure for a 1.5 L engine at 2000 rev/min: throttled at 0.50 bar intake and 1.05 bar exhaust, pumping work per cycle = 0.55 × 10⁵ × 1.5 × 10⁻³ = 82.5 J, or 82.5 × 16.7 = 1375 W; unthrottled at 0.95 bar, 15 J or 250 W. The saving, 1125 W, is 7.5 % of a 15 kW output.

Divided-chamber engine (sketch: cylinder, head with a small pre-chamber holding the plug and a small auxiliary valve, nozzle to the main chamber, main intake valve, piston). In the Honda CVCC type the auxiliary valve admits a rich mixture to the pre-chamber while the main valve admits a lean one. The plug fires the rich mixture easily; it burns and its pressure drives flame jets (a torch) through the nozzle into the lean main charge, which they ignite at many points.

Worked figure: 0.05 g of air at an air–fuel ratio of 12 in the pre-chamber (0.00417 g fuel) and 0.50 g at 22 in the main chamber (0.02273 g) give 0.55 ÷ 0.0269 = 20.4 overall, λ = 1.39, while the plug sees λ = 0.82.

Open-chamber direct-injection engine. Fuel is injected into the cylinder late in compression so a rich cloud reaches the plug at the spark. Early systems (Texaco TCCS, Ford PROCO) used strong swirl to carry the spray past the plug. Modern stratified GDI uses a shaped piston bowl (wall-guided), the air motion (air-guided) or a precise piezo injector next to the plug (spray-guided). At high load the engine switches to an early injection and a homogeneous λ = 1 charge.

Merits: (1) little or no throttling, so low pumping loss and better part-load economy; (2) lean, cooler gas with a higher ratio of specific heats, so a higher cycle efficiency; (3) lean end gas resists knock, allowing a higher compression ratio; (4) low CO; (5) with a pre-chamber, a wide lean limit.

Demerits: (1) HC from over-lean edges of the cloud and from the pre-chamber crevices; (2) soot from the rich zone near the injector; (3) lean exhaust, so a three-way catalyst cannot remove NOx: a lean NOx trap and low-sulphur fuel are needed; (4) plug fouling and complex control of the cloud over the whole speed range; (5) a third valve or a high-pressure injector adds cost.

Conclusion: stratification turns a petrol engine into a quality-controlled engine like a diesel; its efficiency gain is real, but tighter NOx and particle limits have pushed most makers back to λ = 1 direct injection, while pre-chamber jet ignition has returned for very lean engines.

bank.q: Explain the concept of the low heat rejection (LHR) engine. Describe the methods of insulating the combustion chamber and discuss the effects on performance and emissions.
outline: Heat balance: a quarter to a third of fuel energy to coolant
Thermal barrier coatings (YSZ, 0.3–0.5 mm, bond coat), ceramic inserts, air-gap pistons
ΔT = q t ÷ k
Effects: efficiency gain small, exhaust energy up, volumetric efficiency down, NOx up, delay shorter, oil limit
Suits diesel and turbocompounding, not SI
answer: Concept: in a diesel about a quarter to a third of the fuel energy passes through the chamber walls into the coolant. An LHR engine insulates the surfaces the hot gas touches so this heat stays in the gas. The aim is more work, or hotter exhaust that a turbine can use. The extreme idea, the “adiabatic” engine, would need no cooling system at all.

Methods. (1) Thermal barrier coatings: 0.3 to 0.5 mm of yttria-stabilised zirconia, plasma-sprayed on a metallic bond coat, on the piston crown, head face, valve faces and liner top; conductivity about 1 to 2 W/(m·K), against about 150 for aluminium. (2) Monolithic ceramic parts or inserts (silicon nitride, zirconia) for piston caps, liners and port liners. (3) Air-gap pistons and liners: a separate crown or sleeve leaves a thin air layer as insulation. (4) Low-conductivity metal parts such as a steel crown on an aluminium piston.

answer.text: How much a coating holds, for a mean flux of 0.5 MW/m²:

answer: So the coated surface runs far hotter and the heat flux falls (the figures are a first estimate at fixed flux).

answer.text: Heat balance, worked figure. A diesel with 100 kW of fuel power: brake 33 kW, coolant 30 kW, exhaust 30 kW, other 7 kW. Insulation cuts coolant heat by 40 %, freeing 12 kW; if 15 % of that becomes work:

answer: Brake efficiency rises only from 33.0 to 34.8 %, while exhaust energy rises by a third: the gain comes mainly if a turbocharger or a turbo-compound turbine recovers the exhaust.

Effects on performance. Hot walls heat the incoming air, so volumetric efficiency and power density fall. Ignition delay shortens, so diesel knock and noise fall, and low-cetane fuels (alcohols, vegetable oils) ignite better. Lubricating oil on the liner breaks down above about 250 °C, limiting the wall temperature; coatings can crack and spall under thermal cycling.

Effects on emissions. NOx rises because the gas is hotter. CO and HC usually fall because the quench layers are thinner and the late burn is hotter. Smoke may fall from better burn-out or rise if the lower air density makes the mixture richer.

Conclusion: the LHR engine suits the turbocharged diesel; it is unsuitable for petrol engines, where hot walls cause knock. Today the idea returns as thin temperature-swing coatings that heat and cool within each cycle.

bank.q: Distinguish dual-fuel, bi-fuel and multi-fuel engines. Explain why a gas-diesel dual-fuel engine needs a pilot, and discuss substitution, knock and methane slip.
outline: Definitions with examples
Gas metering: mixer, gas carburettor, port injection (fumigation)
Methane: cetane near zero, long delay at 800–860 K; pilot as ignition source
Substitution and gas energy share; pilot 10–30 %, micro-pilot 1 %
Knock at high load, misfire and slip at light load; multi-fuel compromises
answer: Definitions. Dual fuel: two fuels burn together every cycle; a gas carries most of the energy and a diesel pilot ignites it (a CNG-diesel genset). Bi-fuel: two fuels carried, one burnt at a time (a CNG-petrol car). Multi-fuel: one engine that runs on any one of several liquid fuels (diesel, kerosene, jet fuel) without hardware change.

Gas supply. Gas is mixed with the intake air (fumigation) by a venturi mixer, a gas carburettor with a zero-pressure regulator, or timed port injection. The charge entering the cylinder is a lean, premixed gas–air mixture.

Why a pilot. At a compression ratio of 17 the charge reaches roughly T = 320 × 170.35 ≈ 860 K, about methane’s self-ignition temperature of 810 K. Methane’s cetane number is near zero, so its ignition delay at that temperature is far longer than the few milliseconds near top dead centre. A small diesel injection ignites within its normal delay; the burning pilot sprays act like many spark plugs and start flames through the gas–air charge.

Pilot size. In converted engines the pilot is commonly 10 to 30 % of the fuel energy at high load and more at light load; large gas engines use a micro-pilot of about 1 %. A common-rail injector meters such small pilots accurately.

answer.text: Substitution, worked figure (40 kW; diesel alone 10 kg/h; dual fuel 2.5 kg/h diesel at 42.5 MJ/kg and 6.6 kg/h CNG at 50 MJ/kg):
answer.pre:
diesel substitution = (10 − 2.5) ÷ 10 = 75 %
gas energy share = 330 ÷ (106.25 + 330) = 75.6 %
efficiency: 144 ÷ 425 = 33.9 % (diesel); 144 ÷ 436.25 = 33.0 % (dual fuel)

answer: Knock appears at high load: the premixed charge is large, and with an early pilot, hot intake or high compression ratio the end gas self-ignites before the flames arrive. It caps the gas share at full load.

Light-load penalty and methane slip. At light load the gas–air charge is very lean; flames from the pilot are slow and die out, so CO and unburnt methane rise and efficiency falls. Methane slip is this unburnt methane, plus some from crevices and from short-circuiting during valve overlap. Because methane warms the climate far more per kg than CO2, slip can cancel much of the CO2 benefit. Remedies: a bigger pilot and less gas at light load, partial throttling or hot EGR to enrich the charge, and an oxidation catalyst for methane.

Multi-fuel engines fix a compromise compression ratio (often above 20) so low-cetane fuels ignite, and compensate the pump for fuel density and viscosity; cetane, viscosity, lubricity and volatility set the usable fuel range.
Conclusion: dual fuel saves diesel and CO<sub>2</sub> only in the middle of the load range; knock limits it at the top and slip at the bottom.

bank.q: A 150 kW truck diesel is tested with EGR. CO<sub>2</sub> reads 0.04 % in the ambient air, 2.40 % in the intake manifold and 10.5 % in the exhaust. With this EGR the engine-out NOx is 3.5 g/kWh (as NO<sub>2</sub>), and an SCR removes 92 % of it. The brake specific fuel consumption is 215 g/kWh. Find (a) the EGR rate and the exhaust recirculated per kg of fresh air, (b) the urea and AdBlue flow at full load and the AdBlue as a share of the diesel, (c) the tailpipe NOx against a 0.46 g/kWh limit. Comment on the choice between more EGR and more SCR.
outline: NOx removed 483 g/h = 10.5 mol/h; NH₃ 10.5 mol/h; urea 5.25 mol/h = 315 g/h
AdBlue 970 g/h; diesel 32.25 kg/h; ratio 3.0 %
Tailpipe 0.28 g/kWh, passes
EGR costs PM and fuel; SCR costs AdBlue
answer: Data: P = 150 kW; CO<sub>2</sub> ambient 0.04 %, intake 2.40 %, exhaust 10.5 %; engine-out NOx e = 3.5 g/kWh; SCR efficiency 0.92; bsfc 215 g/kWh.
(a) EGR rate. x = (CO2 intake − CO2 ambient) ÷ (CO2 exhaust − CO2 ambient) = (2.40 − 0.04) ÷ (10.5 − 0.04) = 2.36 ÷ 10.46 = 0.2256, that is 22.6 % of the intake charge.
Exhaust per kg of fresh air: x ÷ (1 − x) = 0.2256 ÷ 0.7744 = 0.291 kg/kg (mole and mass shares taken equal, since the molar masses of air and diesel exhaust are close).

answer.pre:
NOx removed      = 0.92 × 3.5 g/kWh × 150 kW = 483 g/h
moles of NOx     = 483 ÷ 46.0 = 10.50 mol/h
NH<sub>3</sub> needed       = 10.50 mol/h   (4NH<sub>3</sub> + 4NO + O<sub>2</sub> → 4N<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O: one NH<sub>3</sub> per NO)
urea             = 10.50 ÷ 2 = 5.25 mol/h   ((NH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CO + H<sub>2</sub>O → 2NH<sub>3</sub> + CO<sub>2</sub>)
urea mass        = 5.25 × 60.06 = 315 g/h
AdBlue           = 315 ÷ 0.325 = 970 g/h ≈ 0.97 kg/h

answer: Diesel flow: 215 g/kWh × 150 kW = 32 250 g/h = 32.25 kg/h. AdBlue share: 0.97 ÷ 32.25 = 0.030, that is 3.0 % of the diesel.
(c) Tailpipe NOx: 3.5 × (1 − 0.92) = 0.28 g/kWh, below the 0.46 g/kWh limit by (0.46 − 0.28) ÷ 0.46 = 39 %.

Comment. More EGR would cut engine-out NOx and the AdBlue bill, but it lowers the oxygen and temperature for soot burn-out, so PM and DPF regenerations rise, and it costs fuel. More SCR lets the engine run with less EGR and earlier injection, which is better for fuel and PM, at the cost of urea and ammonia-slip control. Makers balance the two at each operating point; at cold start, when the SCR is below about 200 °C, EGR carries the NOx duty.
Check: at 6 g/kWh engine-out with 90 % SCR on a 200 kW engine the same method gives 2.17 kg/h of AdBlue, about 5 % of the diesel, so 3 % here is consistent with the lower engine-out NOx.

bank.q: (a) A petrol engine on a test bed burns 8 kg/h of fuel at φ = 0.95 (stoichiometric air–fuel ratio 14.7) and gives 30 kW. The wet exhaust, molar mass 28.7 kg/kmol, holds 0.6 % CO and 1500 ppm NO. Find the CO and NOx (as NO<sub>2</sub>) in g/kWh. (b) A car with this kind of engine is driven over the 11.0 km cycle with CVS sampling: total diluted volume 160 m³; bag CO 45 ppm (background 1 ppm); bag NOx 2.5 ppm (background 0.1 ppm). Densities at standard conditions: CO 1.25 kg/m³, NO<sub>2</sub> 2.05 kg/m³. Judge the car against 1.0 g/km CO and 0.06 g/km NOx.
outline: AFR 15.47; air 123.8 kg/h; exhaust 131.8 kg/h; 4.592 kmol/h
CO 0.772 kg/h = 25.7 g/kWh; NOx 0.317 kg/h = 10.6 g/kWh
CVS: CO 8.8 g = 0.80 g/km, passes
NOx 0.787 g = 0.072 g/km, fails by 19 %
ppm alone cannot decide; engine-out vs tailpipe
answer: (a) Exhaust flow. Air–fuel ratio = 14.7 ÷ 0.95 = 15.47. Air = 15.47 × 8 = 123.8 kg/h. Exhaust = 123.8 + 8 = 131.8 kg/h. Molar flow = 131.8 ÷ 28.7 = 4.592 kmol/h.

answer.text: Gas flows (ppm and per cent are mole fractions):

answer: Brake-specific: CO = 772 g/h ÷ 30 kW = 25.7 g/kWh; NOx = 317 g/h ÷ 30 kW = 10.6 g/kWh. These are engine-out values, before the catalyst.
(b) Cycle masses. The CVS bag holds diluted exhaust; subtract the dilution-air background (simple method) and multiply by the total diluted volume.
NOx exceeds the limit by (0.0716 − 0.06) ÷ 0.06 = 19 %. The car must cut its cycle NOx by 0.787 − 0.06 × 11.0 = 0.127 g, or 16 %.

Why the numbers look so different: the test-bed values are engine-out concentrations of percent or thousands of ppm; the tailpipe after a warm three-way catalyst is tens of ppm, and diluted about ten times in the CVS it reads only a few ppm. A ppm reading tells nothing about pass or fail until it is turned into a mass with the gas volume and density, and divided by the cycle distance (g/km) or work (g/kWh).
Likely fixes for the NOx: tighter closed-loop λ control during transients, a faster-lighting catalyst, or more rhodium loading; the cold start and the high-speed part of the cycle are where to look.

Check the CO arithmetic another way: 0.80 g/km × 11.0 km = 8.8 g, and 8.8 g ÷ 1.25 kg/m³ = 7.04 litres of CO, which is 44 ppm of 160 m³. Check: 0.80 g/km CO is consistent with the cold-start-dominated CO of a catalyst car; the NOx failure by 0.012 g/km is small in mass but decisive against the limit.

bank.q: A 100 kW genset burns 26 kg/h of diesel (LHV 42.5 MJ/kg, 3.16 kg CO<sub>2</sub> per kg). Converted to dual fuel at the same power it burns 6 kg/h of diesel and 17.5 kg/h of CNG (LHV 50 MJ/kg, 2.74 kg CO<sub>2</sub> per kg). Find the diesel substitution, the gas energy share, the brake thermal efficiency in both modes and the CO<sub>2</sub> per kWh. Then assume 2 % of the gas slips through unburnt and that methane warms the climate about 28 times as much as CO<sub>2</sub> per kg over 100 years: what is left of the CO<sub>2</sub> saving?
outline: Substitution 76.9 %; gas share 77.4 %
Efficiency 32.6 % and 31.9 %
Slip 0.35 kg/h: 9.8 kg/h CO₂-equivalent; saving falls to 7.8 %
Slip control decides the climate benefit
answer: Brake output in energy units: 100 kW × 3.6 = 360 MJ/h.

answer.pre:
diesel only:  26 × 42.5 = 1105 MJ/h
dual fuel:    diesel 6 × 42.5 = 255 MJ/h; gas 17.5 × 50 = 875 MJ/h; total 1130 MJ/h

answer: Diesel substitution = (26 − 6) ÷ 26 = 0.769, that is 76.9 %. Gas energy share = 875 ÷ 1130 = 0.774, that is 77.4 %.
Efficiency: diesel only 360 ÷ 1105 = 32.6 %; dual fuel 360 ÷ 1130 = 31.9 %. Dual fuel is slightly less efficient, as usual: part of the lean gas charge burns late or not at all.

Saving with all gas burnt: (82.16 − 66.91) ÷ 82.16 = 0.186, that is 18.6 %. It comes from methane’s lower carbon per MJ (0.0549 against about 0.074 kg/MJ for diesel), partly eaten by the lower efficiency.

answer.pre:
methane slipped     = 0.02 × 17.5 = 0.35 kg/h
CO<sub>2</sub> from burnt gas  = 0.98 × 47.95 = 46.99 kg/h
CO<sub>2</sub>-equivalent of slip = 0.35 × 28 = 9.80 kg/h
total               = 18.96 + 46.99 + 9.80 = 75.75 kg/h
saving              = (82.16 − 75.75) ÷ 82.16 = 7.8 %

answer: So a 2 % slip removes more than half of the climate benefit (18.6 % falls to 7.8 %). (The engine would also need a little more gas to make up the lost energy, which is ignored here.)
Control: keep the gas share lower at light load, enlarge the pilot, reduce valve overlap, and fit an oxidation catalyst coated for methane; measure slip with a heated FID and a non-methane cutter.

Check: CO<sub>2</sub> per MJ of fuel energy is 82.16 ÷ 1105 = 0.0744 kg/MJ on diesel and 66.91 ÷ 1130 = 0.0592 kg/MJ in dual fuel, a 20 % cut per MJ; the stack saving is smaller, 18.6 %, because the dual-fuel engine needs 2 % more fuel energy for the same 100 kW.

Conclusion: dual fuel replaces about three-quarters of the diesel and cuts CO<sub>2</sub> by about a fifth at the stack, but the real climate gain depends on holding methane slip to a fraction of a per cent.

bank.q: An engine is to run first in HCCI mode and then in RCCI mode. Describe the operating strategy, the variable that sets ignition timing and the expected emissions in each case. Use the ignition-delay law τ = A exp(E/RT) with E/R = 15 000 K to show how sensitive HCCI is to a 50 K change from 900 K, and find the global PRF of an RCCI charge of 24 mg iso-octane and 6 mg n-heptane.
outline: HCCI: lean premixed, self-ignition, no flame; levers indirect
HCCI emissions: NOx and soot near zero; HC, CO high at light load; ringing at high load
RCCI: port low-reactivity + direct high-reactivity; ratio and timing set ignition; PRF 80
RCCI wider load range; still needs oxidation catalyst
answer: HCCI strategy. Fuel is premixed with air (port injection or early direct injection) to a lean charge, φ about 0.2 to 0.5, or diluted with EGR. Compression heats the whole charge to self-ignition; there is no spark and no flame front, so the charge burns almost at once.

What sets HCCI timing. Only the chemistry: the ignition delay falls steeply with charge temperature. Levers are indirect: intake temperature, EGR rate, trapped hot residual gas by variable valve timing, compression ratio and fuel reactivity.
A 50 K warmer charge ignites 2.4 times sooner; even 10 K moves the burn by crank degrees, so HCCI needs intake temperature control to a few kelvin.

HCCI emissions. NOx near zero, because no parcel exceeds about 2000 K; soot near zero, because no parcel is rich. HC and CO are high at light load, since the coolest charge near the walls and in crevices never finishes reacting. At high load the whole charge burns too fast (ringing, a very high rate of pressure rise), which sets the upper load limit.

RCCI strategy. A low-reactivity fuel (petrol, ethanol or natural gas) is port-injected to form a lean premixed charge; a high-reactivity fuel (diesel) is injected directly, early enough to mix partly. Ignition starts in the parcels richest in diesel and spreads through the reactivity gradient, so the heat release is spread over more crank angle.

answer.text: What sets RCCI timing: the ratio of the two fuels and the diesel injection timing, both changeable every cycle.
answer.pre:
premixed ratio = 24 ÷ (24 + 6) = 0.80
global PRF     = 100 × 0.80 + 0 × 0.20 = 80
at high load, 27 + 3 mg: ratio 0.90, PRF 90 → less reactive, later and slower burn

answer: RCCI emissions. Low NOx and soot as in HCCI; HC and CO still significant at light load, so a diesel oxidation catalyst is needed; the pressure rise is gentler, so the load range is wider.
Conclusion: both keep the burn inside the lean, cool window of the φ–T map; RCCI adds a usable control lever, which is why research engines reach diesel-like efficiency over a wider range with it.

bank.q: Analyse the trade-off between NOx and soot in a direct-injection diesel engine using the φ–T map, and explain how low-temperature combustion (PCCI, HCCI, RCCI) escapes it.
outline: φ–T map: soot island φ > 2, 1600–2600 K; NOx above about 2200 K at φ ≤ 1
Diesel spray path crosses both
Levers: EGR and retard cut NOx, raise soot; more air, pressure, advance cut soot, raise NOx
LTC: lean or well-mixed, peak below about 2000 K
Costs: ignition control, HC and CO, ringing, load range; after-treatment still needed
answer: The map. Plot every small parcel of in-cylinder gas by its local equivalence ratio φ and local temperature T. Soot forms in an island of rich, hot states, roughly φ above 2 at 1600 to 2600 K. Thermal NO forms where the gas is hotter than about 2200 K with oxygen to spare, near or below φ = 1. (Sketch: T across, φ up; the soot island upper middle, the NOx band lower right.)

Path of a conventional diesel spray. Fuel enters cold and very rich, heats as it mixes, and passes through the soot island in the spray core. The diffusion flame round the jet burns near stoichiometric at 2500 K or more, which is inside the NOx band. One spray therefore makes both pollutants.

head: Change
Effect on the path
NOx
Soot
rows: up: less time to burn out

answer: Each lever moves the spray out of one region and towards the other, so a plot of soot against NOx for a set of settings is a curve running from high NOx–low soot to low NOx–high soot: the trade-off curve.

How LTC escapes. The idea is to keep every parcel out of both regions at once: (1) mix the fuel before it burns, so no parcel is rich (φ below about 1, often 0.2 to 0.5); (2) dilute with EGR or excess air, so the peak stays below about 2000 K. Then the path never enters the soot island or the NOx band.

PCCI injects one fuel early so it partly premixes; the core is smaller, soot and NOx both fall, but some rich parcels remain. HCCI premixes fully and self-ignites by compression; NOx and soot are near zero. RCCI premixes a low-reactivity fuel and adds a high-reactivity fuel directly; the reactivity gradient spreads the burn and gives a control lever.

Worked figure on control: with τ = A exp(E/RT) and E/R = 15 000 K, raising the charge from 900 to 950 K shortens the delay 2.4 times, which shows why timing drifts and why RCCI’s fuel ratio (for example PRF 80 at part load, PRF 90 at high load) is valuable.

Costs of LTC. Ignition is set by chemistry, not by a spark or injection; HC and CO rise because the cool lean charge near the walls does not finish burning; the burn can be too fast at high load (ringing); the load range is limited; and a diesel oxidation catalyst is still needed for HC and CO.

Conclusion: the trade-off belongs to the diffusion flame, not to the diesel engine as such; by moving the burn into the lean, cool corner of the map, LTC lowers both pollutants together, at the price of control.

bank.q: Evaluate whether a three-way catalytic converter alone can control the emissions of a lean-burn or stratified-charge petrol engine, and discuss the alternatives.
outline: TWC needs reductants for NO, so works only within about ±0.5 % of λ = 1
Lean exhaust: CO, HC oxidised; NO not reduced
Alternatives: LNT with rich purges; urea SCR; λ = 1 operation with EGR; GPF for particles
Costs: fuel for purges, sulphur, urea tank, complexity
Judgement: the efficiency gain must pay for the extra after-treatment
answer: How the TWC works. At λ = 1 it oxidises CO and HC with oxygen and reduces NO with the CO, H2 and HC in the same gas, for example 2NO + 2CO → N2 + 2CO2. Both jobs succeed only in a narrow window, about ±0.5 % of λ = 1 (air–fuel ratio about 14.6 to 14.8), held by oxygen sensors and closed-loop injection.

Lean exhaust. A stratified or lean-burn engine runs at λ = 1.3 to 2 or more (for example λ = 1.39 for an overall air–fuel ratio of 20.4). The exhaust holds several per cent oxygen. The CO and HC are oxidised, but the oxygen uses up the reductants before they can reach the NO, so NO passes almost unconverted. A TWC alone therefore controls CO and HC but not NOx.

Is engine-out NOx low enough anyway? Lean operation does lower NO compared with the peak at φ = 0.9, and very lean or diluted charges lower it further, but stratified engines have near-stoichiometric burning zones round the plug, so engine-out NOx stays far above a limit such as 0.06 g/km. The TWC alone fails.

head: Option
How it works
Cost or limit
rows: stores NO<sub>2</sub> as barium nitrate while lean; a rich pulse of a few seconds every minute or so reduces it
fuel for purges (part of the lean gain), sulphur poisoning needs low-sulphur fuel and hot desulphation
NH<sub>3</sub> reduces NOx in lean gas
an AdBlue tank and dosing on a car; works from about 200 °C
Return to λ = 1 with heavy cooled EGR
keeps the TWC; EGR reduces throttling and knock
smaller efficiency gain than lean burn
for the soot of a rich zone in a DI engine

answer: A usable lean petrol line is TWC (for cold start and stoichiometric modes) plus LNT, with 10 ppm sulphur fuel; NOx sensors after the LNT decide when to purge.

Evaluation. The lean engine saves, for example, about 7.5 % of the output in pumping loss at part load, plus some cycle efficiency. The LNT purges, the desulphation events and the extra precious metal take back part of this, and real-driving tests show the purges are hard to keep efficient over the whole map. This is why many makers dropped stratified lean operation when Euro 6 and BS-VI limits and particle-number limits came, and moved to λ = 1 direct injection with cooled EGR, where a TWC and a GPF suffice.
Conclusion: no, a TWC alone cannot control a lean engine’s NOx; lean burn is worth its gain only with an LNT or SCR, and today the cost of that after-treatment usually outweighs the benefit in cars.

bank.q: A city replaces its diesel buses with CNG buses and later tightens its standard to BS-VI. Evaluate the emission and practical consequences of each step, using formation chemistry, after-treatment needs, storage and the driving cycle.
outline: CNG: premixed SI, near-zero soot, CO₂ per MJ 22 % below petrol; NOx and methane remain
Storage: 200 bar, 8.4 MJ/L; refuelling network
BS-VI: CNG with TWC at λ = 1; diesel with DOC + DPF + SCR + 10 ppm fuel
Urban cycle: idle, cold start, low exhaust temperature hurt SCR
Judgement: fuel change and after-treatment are complementary
answer: Step 1: diesel to CNG. A CNG bus engine is a spark-ignition engine burning a premixed gas. With no liquid spray there is no rich core, so soot and PM almost vanish: the visible black smoke of old diesel buses disappears, the main local health gain. Methane carries less carbon per unit energy, 0.0549 kg CO2/MJ against about 0.074 for diesel, but a spark-ignition engine is less efficient than a diesel, so the tailpipe CO2 per km saving is smaller than the fuel figures suggest.

What remains: NOx, because the premixed flame is hot; and unburnt methane, which an ordinary catalyst barely oxidises and which warms the climate about 28 times as much as CO<sub>2</sub> per kg over 100 years. Lean-burn CNG engines of the first generation, with only an oxidation catalyst, had high NOx.

Practical side. CNG is stored at 200 bar with real density about 168 kg/m³ at 15 °C, so a litre of cylinder holds about 8.4 MJ, against 35.7 MJ for a litre of diesel. Buses need many roof cylinders, the range falls, and the city needs compressor stations and a gas pipeline; cylinders need periodic testing. Fuel cost per km is usually lower, and India’s large CNG fleets show the change is workable.

Step 2: BS-VI. For CNG buses, the engine moves to stoichiometric operation with a three-way catalyst coated for methane and closed-loop λ control, which removes NOx, CO and most methane together; this is a modest, cheap step. For any remaining diesel buses BS-VI demands the full line: DOC, DPF, urea dosing and SCR, a slip catalyst and on-board diagnostics, plus 10 ppm sulphur fuel. Limits move to about 0.46 g/kWh NOx and 0.01 g/kWh PM on the transient engine cycle, with particle-number limits.

answer.text: Worked figures to compare the two routes:
answer.pre:
diesel PM: 0.108 g/kWh engine-out → filter must catch 1 − 0.01/0.108 = 91 %
diesel NOx: 6 g/kWh engine-out, 90 % SCR on 200 kW → AdBlue 2.17 kg/h, about 5 % of the diesel
CNG CO<sub>2</sub> per MJ: 22 % below petrol, about 26 % below diesel per MJ of fuel

answer: The driving cycle. A city bus route is close to the slow urban part of a cycle: long idle, frequent stops, low speed and low exhaust temperature. That is the worst case for diesel after-treatment: the SCR needs about 200 °C and the DPF needs heat to regenerate, so urban buses spend long periods with cold catalysts, and real NOx can exceed the certificate. A stoichiometric CNG engine with a TWC stays hot enough more easily. The cycle therefore decides whether the benefit appears in real g/km.

Judgement: the fuel change attacked the pollutant that the diesel made worst, smoke, before after-treatment could; BS-VI then closed the NOx and methane gaps. Neither step alone is enough: the fuel change and the after-treatment are complementary, and for an urban duty cycle a stoichiometric CNG bus with a TWC is the simpler way to meet BS-VI, provided methane slip and leaks are kept low.

bank.q: Stratified charge, low heat rejection, HCCI and RCCI engines are all attempts to raise efficiency. Compare their principles, efficiency gains, emissions and practical problems, and judge which are most promising.
outline: Stratified: rich at plug, lean overall, no throttle; ≈ 7.5 % pumping saving; NOx needs LNT
LHR: insulated chamber; small brake gain, exhaust energy up; NOx up, oil limit
HCCI: lean premixed self-ignition; near-zero NOx and soot; no timing control, ringing, HC and CO
RCCI: two fuels, reactivity gradient; control lever, wider range; two fuel tanks
Judgement with a comparison table
answer: Where the losses are: a part-load petrol engine loses work to pumping and to the slow, hot, stoichiometric burn; a diesel loses a quarter to a third of its fuel energy to the coolant; both lose work when emission controls force retard or rich operation. Each of the four engines attacks one of these losses.

Stratified charge. Principle: a rich zone at the plug lights a lean overall charge, so load is controlled by fuel with the throttle open. Gain: pumping loss falls (worked figure: 1375 W throttled against 250 W unthrottled at 2000 rev/min, a saving of 7.5 % of 15 kW) and the lean cycle is more efficient. Emissions: low CO; HC from lean edges; soot near the injector; NOx cannot be handled by a TWC, so an LNT is needed. Problems: control of the cloud, plug fouling, sulphur sensitivity of the LNT.

LHR. Principle: thermal barrier coatings (0.3 to 0.5 mm zirconia, ΔT about 250 K at 0.5 MW/m²) keep heat in the gas. Gain: small at the shaft (worked figure: 33.0 to 34.8 % when 12 kW of coolant heat is saved), because most saved heat leaves in the exhaust; larger with turbocompounding. Emissions: NOx up from hotter gas; CO and HC down. Problems: hot walls lower volumetric efficiency, oil breaks down above about 250 °C, coatings crack; unsuitable for petrol engines because of knock.

HCCI. Principle: a lean premixed charge self-ignites by compression without a flame. Gain: diesel-like efficiency without throttling and with low heat loss. Emissions: NOx and soot near zero; HC and CO high at light load. Problems: no direct timing control (the delay changes 2.4 times between 900 and 950 K), ringing at high load, a narrow load range, cold start; pure HCCI is not in production, though spark-assisted versions are.

RCCI. Principle: a port-injected low-reactivity fuel and a directly injected high-reactivity fuel; the ratio (for example global PRF 80 at part load, 90 at high load) and the injection timing set the burn. Gain: research engines report diesel-like or better efficiency over a wider load range. Emissions: very low NOx and soot; HC and CO need an oxidation catalyst. Problems: two fuels and two tanks, refuelling habits, transient control; not yet in production.

Judgement: the LHR engine is the least promising as a stand-alone idea, because thermodynamics sends the saved heat to the exhaust; it is useful only with exhaust energy recovery or as modern thin temperature-swing coatings. Stratified charge works but loses its gain to NOx after-treatment under today’s limits; its pre-chamber form survives as jet ignition. HCCI shows the ideal emissions but lacks a control lever. RCCI is the most promising of the four because it keeps HCCI’s low NOx and soot while adding a cycle-by-cycle control, and it fits dual-fuel hardware already used with natural gas, methanol and ethanol.

Conclusion: each idea solves one loss and creates a new problem; the strategies that survive are those, like RCCI and pre-chamber jet ignition, that give back control of when and how fast the charge burns.

glossary.def: a piston whose crown is separated from its body by a thin air layer that insulates it; used in LHR engines.
ammonia that leaves the SCR catalyst unreacted; burnt in a slip catalyst.
an engine that carries two fuels and burns one at a time, such as a CNG-petrol car.
a 0 to 10 reading of how black a filter paper turns after a fixed exhaust volume passes through it.
light given off by a chemical reaction; NO + O₃ gives excited NO₂, whose light measures NO.
a narrow gap, such as the top land above the first ring, that the flame cannot enter.
compound vortex controlled combustion: a divided-chamber stratified charge engine with a rich pre-chamber fed by its own small valve.
a wall-flow honeycomb that traps soot and is cleaned by regeneration.
an engine burning a gas and a diesel pilot together every cycle; the pilot ignites the gas.
actual fuel–air ratio divided by the stoichiometric one; above 1 is rich.
returning part of the exhaust to the intake to cool the flame and lower NOx.
an analyser that burns the sample in a hydrogen flame and measures the ion current, giving HC in ppmC.
homogeneous charge compression ignition: a lean premixed charge that self-ignites by compression, with no flame front.
a catalyst that stores NOx as nitrate in lean running and reduces it during short rich pulses.
the temperature at which a catalyst converts half of a pollutant; about 250 to 300 °C for a three-way catalyst.
an engine with an insulated combustion chamber that sends less heat to the coolant.
unburnt methane leaving a gas or dual-fuel engine.
Modified Indian Driving Cycle: the speed–time trace used to certify cars in India, built on the European NEDC.
non-dispersive infrared analyser for CO and CO₂, using a detector filled with the gas measured.
the share of light blocked by a column of exhaust, in per cent.
all material collected on a filter from diluted exhaust at 47 °C: soot, SOF, sulphate and ash.
premixed charge compression ignition: one fuel injected early so that it partly premixes before it self-ignites.
parts per million of carbon atoms, the unit of an FID reading.
reactivity controlled compression ignition: a port-injected low-reactivity fuel ignited by a directly injected high-reactivity fuel.
a very fast rise of cylinder pressure when a premixed charge burns at once, which limits HCCI at high load.
reduction of NOx to nitrogen by ammonia from urea, on a catalyst in lean exhaust.
unburnt fuel and oil condensed on soot particles.
a charge rich at the spark plug and lean elsewhere, lean overall.
a thin ceramic layer, usually yttria-stabilised zirconia, that insulates a hot engine surface.
a catalyst that oxidises CO and HC and reduces NOx at the same time, only near λ = 1.
